_comment: THE plain-language gloss for every rule the supply-chain scanner can emit, in one
language-neutral place (#2633). What each rule MEANS, in terms of what the content can
then do to this machine. Three finding-row renderers read it and none owns it:
- web/src/lib/scanFindings.ts  — imports this file and vends ruleGloss() to the
app-install consent card and the skills marketplace detail surface;
- personalclaw/supply_chain.py — load_scan_rule_gloss()/rule_gloss(), which
`personalclaw skills install` prints beneath each refused finding.
A RULE NAME IS NOT A DISCLOSURE. `python_exec (warning) — server/provider.py:
subprocess.run([...])` names the pattern and shows the code but never says what the
pattern lets the content do, and a non-expert cannot weigh `python_exec` at all. The
gloss COMPLEMENTS the evidence — the evidence is the concrete argv, this is the
consequence — so it stays one clause and never restates the snippet.
It is disclosure only. Glossing a rule does not soften it: the severity beside it and
the verdict above it are untouched, and a `dangerous` finding reads as terminal either
way. The vocabulary is CLOSED (supply_chain.py's pattern catalogs plus the literal
names at hand-built Finding(...) call sites) and
tests/test_supply_chain_scanner.py::test_every_scanner_rule_has_a_plain_language_gloss
asserts this file covers exactly those — a new rule ships glossed or reds the suite,
because the failure mode here is silence, and silence is what a user reads as
"probably fine".
Key order below groups by band, matching the scanner's own catalogs: terminal
(dangerous) content, then overridable (warning) content, then prompt injection — prose
aimed at the assistant that reads the content's own text.
destructive_root: This code deletes files from the root of the filesystem or your home directory.
destructive_delete: This code erases a folder that your account or this machine depends on.
destructive_walk: This code sweeps a whole folder tree and erases every file it comes across.
destructive_truncate: This code empties out a file that this machine needs in order to work.
fork_bomb: This code spawns processes without limit until the machine stops responding.
disk_wipe: This code writes straight to a raw disk device, destroying what is on it.
remote_exec_pipe: This code downloads more code from the internet and runs it immediately, unread.
obfuscated_exec: This code decodes hidden text and runs it, so what runs cannot be read here.
exfil_sensitive_path: This code reads a credential file and sends its contents off this machine.
bidi_override: Direction-flipping characters hide text here, so what you read is not what runs.
eval_exec: This code builds more code as text while it runs, then executes it.
pipe_to_shell: This code feeds output straight into a shell to be run as commands.
curl_network: This code downloads from the internet while it runs.
sudo_use: This code asks for administrator rights to act as root on this machine.
python_exec: This code runs an external program on your machine.
node_exec: This code runs an external program on your machine.
crontab_write: This code edits this machine's scheduled-job table, so it can keep running later.
reads_sensitive_path: This code reads a file where credentials and keys are kept.
overlong_line: A line here is too long to read in one go, so it was read in overlapping parts. That is common in minified code and unusual anywhere else.
nested_too_deep: This file nests its code deeper than Python itself can read, so it couldn't be checked safely, and no program needs that.
unscanned_file: PersonalClaw could not read this file, so nothing in it was checked and it could hold anything.
zero_width_chars: Invisible characters are present, which can hide text from a reviewer.
quarantine_strip: This tells you to switch off the check macOS makes before a downloaded program first runs.
password_archive: This unpacks a download locked with a password, so nothing inside it was checked before it runs.
paste_site_link: This points to text on a paste service, which can change after you approve the install.
fetch_and_follow: This tells the reader to download text and carry out what it says, which whoever controls that text decides.
credential_in_notes: This asks for a password or key to be kept as plain text in memory or notes, where other work can read it back.
injection_ignore: Text here addresses your assistant and tells it to ignore its own instructions.
injection_disregard: Text here addresses your assistant and tells it to disregard what it was told.
injection_coerce: Text here addresses your assistant and orders it to run or call something.
injection_override: Text here poses as a replacement for your assistant's instructions.

_comment: The sentence for an execution rule found in instructions a PERSON reads and runs (a
README, a prerequisite's how; install_instructions.PROSE), in place of the rule's own,
which speaks of code. Many official installers are a download piped into a shell, so
the sentence says when that is still a reasonable choice (#3852, settled 2026-10-26);
a decoded payload never is. Every key is one of install_instructions.EXECUTION_RULES.
_in_prose.remote_exec_pipe: These steps download a program and run it at once, unread. Many official installers work this way, and that is reasonable when the address is the project's own site.
_in_prose.pipe_to_shell: These steps feed text straight into a shell to be run as commands. An official installer run this way is reasonable when the address is the project's own site.
_in_prose.obfuscated_exec: These steps decode hidden text and run it, so what runs cannot be read here.
